title: Psalm 94: The Judge of the Earth Will Not Forsake His People
summary: The psalm calls on the LORD, the God of vengeance and Judge of the earth, to act against the proud who crush his people, kill widows, foreigners, and orphans, and say that God does not see. It rebukes such fools: the one who made the ear and eye surely hears and sees. It blesses the one whom God disciplines and teaches, and it ends with personal testimony that God's loving devotion held the psalmist up and that God will destroy the wicked for their iniquity.
story: Psalm 94 follows the proclamation of God's kingship in Psalm 93 and precedes the next great cluster of psalms that say “The LORD reigns” (Psalms 95 to 99). Its position is instructive. Having declared that God rules over the floods, the Psalter immediately admits that the world is still full of injustice, and it calls on the King to act as Judge. Book IV was shaped in the shadow of the loss of Israel's monarchy, and this psalm voices the question that loss raised: if God reigns, why do the wicked triumph? The answer is not denial but confidence that God sees, disciplines, and will not abandon his people. The same theme appears in Book III's opening psalm (Psalm 73), where the psalmist's foot nearly slipped over the prosperity of the wicked; here the psalmist's foot slips and God's love holds him up (verse 18).
historical:
The Hebrew text gives Psalm 94 no heading. The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, attributes it to David and assigns it to the fourth day of the week, and the Mishnah (the Jewish legal tradition compiled around AD 200) lists it as the psalm the Levites sang on that day in the Second Temple (Mishnah Tamid 7:4).

The psalm's date and setting are unknown. The oppressors it describes may be foreign powers crushing Israel, since they oppress God's heritage, his people as a whole (verse 5). But several details suggest injustice within Israel: the fools are addressed as “senseless among the people” (verse 8), and verse 20 speaks of “a corrupt throne”, a seat of judgment that devises mischief by decree and condemns the innocent. Many interpreters therefore think the psalm protests against corrupt rulers and judges inside the community, the kind the eighth- and seventh-century prophets condemned for exploiting widows and orphans (Isaiah 10:1-2; Jeremiah 22:3). Some read it as coming from the late monarchy, others from the period after the exile. The psalm is general enough to have been prayed in either setting.
cultural:
The widow, the foreigner, and the fatherless were the classic vulnerable groups in Israelite law. Without a husband, a father, or family land, they had no one to speak for them in the courts at the city gate. The law repeatedly commands their protection and warns that God himself hears their cry (Exodus 22:21-24; Deuteronomy 10:18; 24:17). To kill them, as verse 6 says the wicked do, was a direct assault on the people God had pledged to defend.

In the ancient world, justice depended on the honesty of kings and judges. A corrupt court could condemn the innocent under the cover of law, which is what verse 20 describes: mischief by decree. The claim of the wicked, that God does not see (verse 7), expressed a practical atheism common in every age: not a denial that God exists, but the belief that he doesn't notice or care. Vengeance in the ancient Near East was not primarily personal revenge but the restoration of justice by legitimate authority. To call God the God of vengeance was to appeal to the highest court.
literary: Psalm 94 combines three kinds of material. Verses 1 to 7 are a communal lament addressed to God, asking how long the wicked will triumph and quoting their boast. Verses 8 to 15 are wisdom teaching, turning to address the fools directly with rhetorical questions (“He who affixed the ear, can He not hear?”) and blessing the person God disciplines. Verses 16 to 23 are individual testimony and confidence, in which the psalmist speaks of his own near brush with death and of God's support. The opening repeats its key phrase for emphasis: “O LORD, God of vengeance, O God of vengeance”. The question “How long” in verse 3 is matched by the fool's question in verse 8, “when will you be wise?”. The psalm moves from public complaint to personal assurance, and ends where it began, with God acting against the wicked.

outline.t: Rise up, Judge of the earth
The arrogant crush God's people and say he does not see
Fools rebuked: the maker of eye and ear sees and hears
Blessed is the one God disciplines
God's love held me when my foot slipped
No alliance with a corrupt throne; the LORD my refuge

doctrines.note: God is the Judge of the earth who sees every injustice and will repay the proud. The psalm treats his vengeance not as cruelty but as the restoration of justice for those who have no other defender.
The one who formed the eye and planted the ear sees and hears. Nothing done in secret escapes God's knowledge, and he knows even the futility of human thoughts.

The psalm holds together discipline and deliverance: God teaches his people through hardship, gives them rest from days of trouble, and holds them up when their foot slips. He will never abandon his heritage.

words.note: Neqamah, vengeance. In the Old Testament it usually refers to the just punishment of wrongdoing by a rightful authority, not private revenge. The law forbids Israelites to take vengeance on one another (Leviticus 19:18), and God reserves it to himself (Deuteronomy 32:35). The psalm asks God to do what individuals may not.

Yasar, to discipline or instruct. It covers correction, training, and teaching, the way a parent shapes a child. Verse 10 argues that the God who disciplines the nations surely knows what is happening, and verse 12 blesses the person God disciplines and teaches from his law.

Nachalah, heritage or inheritance. Israel is God's own inheritance, the people he took as his possession (Deuteronomy 32:9). The oppressors crush God's heritage in verse 5, and verse 14 promises that he will never abandon it.

Sarap, anxious or disquieting thoughts. It appears only here and in Psalm 139:23. Verse 19 speaks of an abundance of such thoughts, and of God's consolations delighting the soul in the middle of them.

christ: Paul quotes verse 11 in 1 Corinthians 3:20 to warn against human pride in wisdom: the Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile. In Romans 11:1-2 he echoes verse 14 to insist that God has not rejected his people, even as Gentiles are brought in. More broadly, the psalm's cry for the Judge of the earth to rise up and set things right finds its New Testament answer in the risen Christ, whom God has appointed to judge the world in righteousness (Acts 17:31). The New Testament also shows Jesus as the innocent one condemned by a corrupt court, a throne of mischief by decree, and vindicated by God. Paul's command not to take vengeance but to leave room for God's wrath (Romans 12:19, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35) reflects the psalm's pattern: justice is entrusted to God, not seized by his people.

hard.q: How can Christians pray to the “God of vengeance”?
hard.a:
The phrase makes modern readers uneasy, because vengeance sounds like personal revenge. But in the Old Testament, vengeance is primarily the just action of a rightful authority to punish wrong and restore those who were harmed. The psalm asks God to do this because human courts have failed: the widow and orphan are being killed, and the judges are corrupt. Calling on the God of vengeance is an appeal for justice, not permission for private retaliation, which the law forbids (Leviticus 19:18).

The New Testament does not abandon this language. Paul tells believers not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35 (Romans 12:19), and Revelation pictures the martyrs asking how long before God avenges their blood (Revelation 6:10). Some Christians emphasize that God's justice has been satisfied at the cross for all who repent, so that the prayer for vengeance becomes a prayer for evil to end and for oppressors to be stopped or converted. Others emphasize that a God who never judged would be indifferent to victims. These views often stand together: the church prays for its enemies and also for God to put the world right.

questions: The wicked say, “The LORD does not see.” Where do you see people living as though God doesn't notice, and where might you be tempted to do the same?
Verse 12 calls the one God disciplines blessed. How have hard seasons taught you something you could not have learned otherwise?
The psalm protests injustice against widows, foreigners, and orphans. Who are the most vulnerable in your community, and what does this psalm ask of those who have power to protect them?
